claims.text: Engineered multilayer interfaces act as barriers to stress-assisted dislocation climb and associated lattice-diffusion processes.
Barrier action by multilayer interfaces reduces time-dependent plastic deformation and creep.
Multilayer interfaces generate local stress fields.
Multilayer interfaces impede continuous diffusion paths.
Interface-generated stress fields and interrupted diffusion paths restrict dislocation climb.
The multilayer interfaces restrict dynamic recrystallization.
Chemical and structural heterogeneity in alternating layers reduces the effective diffusion length relevant to dislocation climb.
Alternating layers induce localized back-stresses that impede dislocation climb.
Interface barriers increase the activation energy for creep.
Stress-assisted dislocation climb controlled by lattice diffusion can govern creep in a high-entropy alloy.
Temperatures of approximately 500–600 °C place the proposed multilayer coatings in a lattice-diffusion and dislocation-climb creep regime.
The multilayer coating will have a significantly lower creep strain rate than a comparable monolithic HEA coating.
The multilayer coating will have a higher estimated creep activation energy than a comparable monolithic HEA coating.
Post-creep microscopy will show dislocation motion constrained near multilayer interfaces.
Multilayer interfaces will remain largely intact under the proposed creep conditions.
The proposed mechanism ceases to be effective at temperatures high enough to destroy interface integrity.
Significant dynamic recrystallization may define a regime in which the interface-barrier mechanism is no longer controlling.
